title: Chocolate sail shards
subtitle: thin sheets of tempered chocolate set on baking paper and broken into irregular shards for cake decoration
excerpt: Chocolate sails and shards are made by spreading melted, tempered chocolate thinly over baking paper and leaving it to set at room temperature. Once firm, the sheet is peeled away and broken into irregular pieces. The shards can be plain, marbled, or finished with lustre dust, dried flowers, or flaked salt.
sourceNotes: Chocolate decorations of this type have been used in French patisserie for decades. The modern practice of setting chocolate on baking paper or acetate to produce decorative shards became popular in British restaurant pastry and home baking during the 2010s.

content.text: Chocolate sails and shards are made from tempered chocolate spread thinly over baking paper, then broken into pieces once set. Proper tempering gives the chocolate a glassy, snapping finish rather than a dull, crumbly one. Dark chocolate tempers most reliably; milk and white chocolate are softer and need a lower working temperature.
Chop 200 g of dark chocolate finely. Melt two-thirds over a bain-marie (a bowl set over barely simmering water, the bowl not touching the water). Heat to 50 to 55 degrees C. Remove from the heat.

Stir in the remaining finely chopped chocolate a handful at a time. This cools the mass and seeds the temper. Stir until the chocolate reaches 31 to 32 degrees C. It should be glossy and flow smoothly off the spatula.

Pour the tempered chocolate onto a sheet of baking paper on a flat tray. Spread immediately with a palette knife or icing spatula to an even layer, about 2 to 3 mm thick. Work quickly before the chocolate starts to set.
Add decoration while the surface is still wet: flaked salt, dried edible flowers, gold lustre, or drops of a second colour of chocolate. For a marbled effect, drag a toothpick through the surface.

Leave at room temperature for at least 1 hour until completely set. Do not refrigerate during setting as cold air can cause fat bloom. Once firm, peel away the baking paper and break into shards of whatever size you need.
Press the shards into the top of a frosted cake at varying angles. Handle as little as possible; fingerprints mark the surface. Store in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 2 weeks.

attrs.problem: Chocolate dull, grey, and crumbly rather than snapping cleanly
attrs.avoid: Avoid working with chocolate that is above 32 degrees C (dark); it will have lost its temper.
attrs.fix: Check the temperature before spreading. If it has gone above 32 degrees C, return to the bain-marie, remelt to 50 degrees C, and re-temper from the start.

attrs.problem: White streaks or spots appearing on the surface after setting
attrs.avoid: Avoid refrigerating the chocolate while it sets; the temperature shock causes fat bloom.
attrs.fix: Leave to set at room temperature between 18 and 20 degrees C. If the room is warm, move the tray to the coolest spot available rather than the fridge.
